title: Ellington's men who wrote tunes and never got credit
summary: Hodges, Brown, Hardwick, Cootie and Rex wrote numbers that went out under Duke's and Irving Mills's names for $25 or $50 and by the time they learned better it was too late.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: MS. WILLARD: Like what? What do you mean? What kind of things?

MR. BIGARD: Oh, like take credit for things that he didn't do. You know, things like that, instead of giving the guys that really did it, you know, give them a mention. Mention their name and let them know that they had a part in this thing. You know, a fellow like Hodges, Brown, Otto Hardwick and Cootie and Rex, they all wrote numbers, composing them, and then he took advantage of it and it was Duke.
MS. WILLARD: Did anybody ever argue with him?

No, they did it like it was -- they'd give them a little payoff, you know. And during that time they'd give you $50 or $25. I mean, the guy was, he was satisfied with it. He wouldn't say anymore about it. And Irving Mills would have his name on it and he didn't write the first note or nothing. And so that's when the guys, as they grew older and they began to learn more from different music writers how they do those things, then they began to get wise, and then there was a different story altogether, see.

But it was too late because the main -- the hit tunes that they had written themselves, I mean, they never did get credit for it and never did make any money off it, you know. So that was bad things like that.
